passages.happening:
The chapter begins with Aaron's family. He had four sons: ‘Nadab the firstborn, then Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar’ (verse 2). Two of them are gone. “Nadab and Abihu, however, died in the presence of the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai” (verse 4). Only Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests beside their father.

Then God gives the tribe of Levi to Aaron as helpers. “They shall take care of all the furnishings of the Tent of Meeting” (verse 8). The priesthood itself stays with Aaron and his sons (verse 10).

God gives the reason. “Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn Israelite from the womb. The Levites belong to Me, for all the firstborn are Mine” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 1 and 2 left the tribe of Levi out of the count. Now the book explains why.

There are two groups here, and it helps to keep them apart. The priests are Aaron and his sons. They offer the sacrifices. The Levites are the rest of the tribe. They assist the priests and look after the tent. Large temples in the ancient world had staffs arranged in the same way, with senior priests who performed the rites and lower orders who kept the doors and the stores.

The memory of Nadab and Abihu hangs over the opening verses. The story is told in Leviticus 10. The word for their ‘unauthorized’ fire is the same Hebrew word used in verse 10 for the ‘outsider’ who must not come near. What does not belong to God's appointed order, whether fire or person, may not approach. In these chapters ‘outsider’ means anyone who is not of the priestly family, other Israelites included.

The reason for the Levites' place goes back to the night Israel left Egypt. God struck down the firstborn of Egypt and spared the firstborn of Israel, and from that night he claimed Israel's firstborn as his own (Exodus 13:13-15). A firstborn son held a special place in every ancient family. Some of Israel's neighbors gave firstborn sons to their gods in the most terrible way; the Bible records a king of Moab offering his firstborn son on a city wall (2 Kings 3:27). Israel's law starts from the same belief, that the firstborn belong to God, and then refuses the sacrifice. Firstborn sons were always bought back. Here a whole tribe is given to God's service in place of every family's eldest son.

How the line between priests and Levites developed is debated. Deuteronomy speaks of ‘the Levitical priests’ (Deuteronomy 18:1). Julius Wellhausen and many scholars after him held that the sharp line was drawn late, after the exile, and written back into the wilderness. Others answer that Deuteronomy's phrase names the priests' tribe without removing the line, and that the duties in Numbers, tied to clans and to a tent that is carried, fit a people on the move. These notes do not settle it.
passages.later:
God called the whole nation his firstborn when he sent Moses to Pharaoh: ‘Israel is My firstborn son’ (Exodus 4:22).

Luke tells how Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple under this law. He cites it: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord” (Luke 2:23).

Hebrews notes that Jesus was not a Levite: “For it is clear that our Lord descended from Judah, a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests” (Hebrews 7:14). His priesthood is of a different kind.
passages.asks: God said of the Levites, ‘They are Mine.’ Ask what in your life you treat as wholly your own: your time, your children, your work. And ask what it would change to hear God say of you what he said of them.

passages.t: Three clans, and what each one carried
passages.happening:
God tells Moses to count the Levites, ‘every male a month old or more’ (verse 15). Levi had three sons, Gershon, Kohath and Merari, and the tribe is counted by their clans.

The Gershonites number 7,500. They camp on the west, behind the tabernacle, and care for its curtains and coverings (verses 21-26). The Kohathites camp on the south. “Their duties were the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the articles of the sanctuary used with them, and the curtain” (verse 31). The clans of Merari camp on the north and care for the frames, crossbars, posts and bases (verses 36-37).

Moses, Aaron and Aaron's sons camp on the east, before the entrance (verse 38). The Levites number 22,000 in all (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
The census of the Levites differs from the census of chapter 1. The other tribes counted men of twenty and over, because that count was for war. The Levites are counted from one month old, because they stand in place of the firstborn, and a firstborn son belongs to God from his first weeks.

Each clan gets the same short entry: its families, its number, its place in the camp, its leader and its work. With this chapter the picture of the camp is complete. The priests and Levites surround the tent on four sides, and the twelve tribes camp beyond them.

Notice how ordinary most of the work is. One clan carries curtains and ropes. Another carries posts, bases and tent pegs. Only the Kohathites carry the holy furniture. But the text gives each clan the same care, and of each it says the same words: ‘all the service for these items’. A tent peg, carried for God, is part of his service.

There is a seed of later trouble in the list. Among the Kohathites, who carry the holiest things, is the clan of Izhar (verse 27). Korah, who will lead a revolt against Aaron in chapter 16, is a son of Izhar.

Readers who add the figures will notice that 7,500, 8,600 and 6,200 make 22,300, while verse 39 gives 22,000. The hard question below takes this up.
passages.later:
Chronicles shows the same three clans, Gershon, Kohath and Merari, still serving when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:4-10).

Paul uses the picture of many members with different tasks for the church: “But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design” (1 Corinthians 12:18).
passages.hard:
The three clans add up to 22,300, but verse 39 says 22,000. Which is right?

The difference is plain, and the sums in the next passage depend on the lower total. Readers have explained it in several ways.

One common explanation is a slip in copying the number for Kohath. In Hebrew the words for three and six differ by a single letter. If Kohath first had 8,300 and not 8,600, everything adds up.

An old Jewish explanation, found in the Talmud and repeated by the medieval commentator Rashi, is that the extra 300 were themselves firstborn Levites. They belonged to God already, so they could not stand in for anyone else.

Others simply note that the ancient text gives round figures in places.

None of these answers changes anything the chapter teaches. The difference is a reminder that Scripture was copied by hand for thousands of years, and that careful readers, Jewish and Christian, have always noticed such details and discussed them openly.
passages.asks: One clan carried the ark and another carried tent pegs, and each was counted and named. Ask which tasks in your church or family you think of as beneath notice. And ask who does that work now, and whether anyone has thanked them.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to count every firstborn male in Israel, a month old or more (verse 40). There are 22,273 (verse 43).

“Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn of Israel, and the livestock of the Levites in place of their livestock. The Levites belong to Me; I am the LORD” (verse 45).

There are 273 more firstborn than Levites. For each of these, five shekels of silver are paid (verses 46-47). Moses collects 1,365 shekels and gives the money to Aaron and his sons, ‘just as the LORD had commanded him’ (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
The chapter now does its arithmetic. One Levite stands for one firstborn son. The 22,000 Levites cover 22,000 of the firstborn. That leaves 273 with no Levite to stand in their place, and for each of them a price is paid.

The Hebrew word for these 273 means ransomed, bought back. The same family of words is used for God buying Israel out of slavery in Egypt. So the payment is a small acting out of the exodus. Each family with a firstborn son is reminded that the boy is alive because God spared him, and that he belongs to God.

The shekel was not a coin. Coins were not invented until centuries later. It was a weight of silver, roughly eleven or twelve grams. Five shekels is the value Leviticus sets for a boy under five (Leviticus 27:6), and it is the price later fixed for redeeming a firstborn son (18:16). Jewish families still mark the redemption of a firstborn son, a month after his birth, in a ceremony based on these laws.

No one's place before God is left to chance in this chapter. Each firstborn is either stood for by a Levite or bought back at a price.
passages.later:
The law of the firstborn was given on the way out of Egypt. A father is told to explain it to his son: ‘I redeem all the firstborn of my sons’ (Exodus 13:15).

Peter takes up the language of a price: “For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18-19). The New Testament draws on this pattern of one life standing in place of another. The chapter itself is not a prediction.
passages.asks: Every firstborn son in Israel was either stood for by another or bought back. Ask whether you live as someone who has been bought back at a cost, or as someone who owes no one anything. And ask how you would explain to a child, in plain words, what it means to belong to God.
